stances.claim: The ICI commissioners deserve appreciation but face structural disadvantages -- 24/7 workload, 16,000+ complaints, no existing organizational backup, salary-standardization compensation, and well-resourced contractor cohorts who can hire the best legal, financial, accounting, tax, banking, and PR experts against them.

Because they are looked upon as model public servants, the commissioners must not merely disclose but actively divest from personal investments, resign from professional and business undertakings, and accept survivalist Salary-Standardization compensation -- and they must publish their SALNs on the ICI website regardless of any other agency's restrictive rulings.

CJ's stronger personal proposal: each commissioner should voluntarily include in his/her SALN a waiver of bank-secrecy protections -- setting by example the very standard they will demand of respondents during investigations.

Even good-faith disclosure cannot be perfect -- relatives with dealings tied to investigation subjects can be scrutinized, pressured, or weaponized against the commissioners -- so the commissioners and their families must be ready to forego their privacy entirely.

Mastery of the Constitution, Ombudsman Law, Anti-Graft Law, Anti-Plunder Law, Ethical Standards Law, Revised Penal Code, and the Administrative Code is not optional but a daily working necessity -- commissioners should carry copies on an iPad, phone, or memo book.

notable_anecdotes: Baguio Mayor Benjamin Magalong's quiet resignation as ICI special adviser -- noted in a single line as the column's only structural change to the commission's roster.

The image of contractors and cohorts hiring the best legal, financial, accounting, tax, banking, and PR experts to face commissioners working under the Salary Standardization Law -- a deliberate resource-asymmetry portrait.
CJ's personally-volunteered upgrade beyond the legal minimum: that commissioners should include in their SALNs a voluntary waiver of bank secrecy, treating SALN as a leadership-by-example artifact.

The reminder that even 'luscious sexual adventures' from the past would be dug up -- not for fitness assessment but for political horse-trading -- a striking phrasing for a constitutional-law columnist.
The vivid 'microscopes, telescopes, and mobile cameras (with their latest killer apps)' metaphor for the surveillance environment a modern commissioner inhabits.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers a sympathetic but exacting profile of the Independent Commission for Infrastructure under chair ret. SC Justice Andres Reyes Jr., with members former DPWH Secretary Rogelio Singson and SGV country managing partner Rossana Fajardo (Baguio Mayor Benjamin Magalong has resigned as special adviser). Their assignment is to help and facilitate -- not interfere with -- the OMB and DOJ in the flood-control accountability drive, but they confront 24/7 workloads, 16,000 forwarded complaints plus thousands more, no existing organizational backup, suits questioning the ICI's very creation, and contractor cohorts with the financial, political, and physical means to hire the best legal, financial, accounting, tax, banking, and PR experts against them. As public officials sworn before the President, they must disclose financial and business interests, divest from personal investments, resign from outside undertakings, and accept Salary-Standardization compensation; CJ goes further, urging them to publish their SALNs on the ICI website regardless of any agency restrictions and to voluntarily include in those SALNs a waiver of bank-secrecy. He acknowledges that even good-faith disclosure cannot be perfect -- relatives can be scrutinized, weaponized, and used as pressure points -- and that commissioners and their families must be ready to forego their privacy under the microscopes, telescopes, and 'killer apps' of modern tri-media and social media, including long-forgotten indiscretions deployed for political horse-trading. The column closes on the constitutional reminder that public office is a public trust requiring modest lives, and a working-toolkit prescription: always carry the Constitution, Ombudsman Law, Anti-Graft Law, Anti-Plunder Law, Ethical Standards Law, Revised Penal Code, and the Administrative Code.
